intro: Rapid flute passagework meets the collective attack of strings in the concerto’s Presto. Only the complete finale is hosted here, not the preceding Allegro di molto and Largo.
question: How does the solo flute turn orchestral material into its own kind of motion?

sections.label: Opening orchestral statement
sections.mNote: ensemble states material before flute becomes an independent soloist

sections.label: Solo and string exchanges
sections.mNote: flute elaboration alternates with orchestral responses

sections.mNote: successive episodes grouped without claiming individual ritornello boundaries

cues.title: The concerto’s last movement
cues.text: This Presto is the third movement of a concerto for flute, strings and continuo. Only the finale is hosted here. Flute and strings share the opening statement before the flute takes a more independent solo role.
cues.evidence: The modern critical performing part writes out the flute’s opening tutti participation, clarifying the condensed manuscript’s blank staff. Its first solo is marked at bar 49. The work has three movements; the critical edition calls the first Allegro di molto. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf (PDF pp. 21–22)

cues.title: Remember the shared gestures
cues.text: Keep the opening gestures in mind as the flute moves from the ensemble into a more independent role. The instrument is not simply arriving for the first time: shared attacks become a reference point for its longer solo line.
cues.evidence: The critical performing part shows flute participation in the opening tutti and the first solo at bar 49. The report has continuous activity through 0:35–0:45 and a lower spectral balance around 0:50; the exact first solo attack is not claimed. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf (PDF pp. 21–22)
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A keyboard player at court
cues.text: Bach’s official appointment as Frederick II’s court harpsichordist begins in 1740. The king plays the flute, but that does not establish him as this concerto’s intended soloist: the recipient of the flute adaptation is unknown.
cues.evidence: The Complete Works chronology gives the 1740 appointment; Barthold Kuijken explicitly states that the flute version’s recipient is unknown. https://www.cpebach.org/timeline/chronology ; https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Breath and continuous motion
cues.text: Across the solo episodes, follow the flute’s running figures against the strings’ shorter interventions. Breath is a compositional constraint here: the line cannot continue indefinitely in the way an organ passage can.
cues.evidence: Kuijken’s introduction explains the adaptation of organ passages and insertion of string interventions for breathing. The manuscript confirms contrasting solo and accompanying textures; no particular breath or intervention is assigned to 1:45. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An organ concerto transformed
cues.text: The secure date 1755 belongs to the original organ concerto, Wq 34. Bach later adapts it for flute as Wq 169, adjusting the range and accompaniment. The flute version’s precise year is not known.
cues.evidence: Kuijken dates the working manuscript between the 1755 organ original and Bach’s departure for Hamburg in 1768. This corrects the upstream programme’s simplified 1755 attribution. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Listen across the replies
cues.text: Through the middle exchanges, distinguish the solo line’s elaboration from the orchestra’s punctuation. A short string response can organise a long stretch without stopping the underlying quick movement.
cues.evidence: The flute-version manuscript and Kuijken’s account document solo–string exchanges. The report has changes near 2:30, 2:40 and 2:56, but does not establish an instrument entrance at 2:55; the suggestion is deliberately passage-level.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Continuity beneath changing harmony
cues.text: Listen to the bass underneath the solo line rather than following the flute alone. Its changing support gives direction to the rapid figures and helps distinguish an excursion from a settled arrival.
cues.evidence: The inspected score has a figured basso line beneath the solo episodes. The report changes strongly around 3:28, but its local key estimates are not sufficient to identify a particular cadence or bass instrument.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A marked withdrawal
cues.text: In this quieter stretch, the recorded level drops sharply and the attacks become more widely spaced. Keep the earlier quick pulse in memory while the sound leaves more room between gestures.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −11.4 dB at 3:55 to −31.9 dB at 4:05 and remains low through 4:15; detected attacks fall to roughly 1–2 per second. This does not identify the precise fermata, an improvised cadenza or individual desks.

cues.title: The arranger’s own handwriting
cues.text: The surviving working score begins as a copy of the keyboard concerto with an empty upper staff. Bach adds the flute line himself and changes accompanying parts. The manuscript preserves adaptation in progress, not simply a change of instrument name.
cues.evidence: Kuijken identifies the copyist as Anon. 303 and Bach’s autograph flute part in Berlin manuscript Mus. ms. Bach P 769. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf

cues.title: The quick motion recovers
cues.text: After the quieter stretch, compare the renewed density of attack with the earlier exchanges. The final part of the movement restores momentum through familiar solo and orchestral resources, not by adding a new instrumental family.
cues.evidence: The report rises after 4:20, with strong changes at 4:54 and 5:04 and a high level window at 5:10. The manuscript supplies the unchanged flute-and-strings forces; the analysis does not identify a particular solo flourish.

cues.title: A shared ending
cues.text: The closing tutti gathers flute and strings into a G-major ending. Compare their shared gestures with the flute’s earlier extended solo runs, then listen to the final resonance after the last cadence.
cues.evidence: The critical flute part writes out participation in the closing tutti; the blank upper staff in the working manuscript does not establish silence. Placement in the last half-minute is approximate; the report remains active through 5:55, then falls to −43.5 dB with no detected attacks at 6:05. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf (PDF p. 29)
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The flute elaborates the orchestral material
transitions.how: The first independent solo follows the opening tutti, in which the flute also participates. Bach gives the solo flute the thematic outline with its own slur and trill, while the strings become a lighter accompaniment. The change of foreground does not require a new tempo or a previously silent instrument.
transitions.evidence: The critical flute part marks the first solo at bar 49 after written tutti participation; Kuijken describes the added slur and trill. The approximate 0:50 division follows the brighter 0:40–0:45 span and lower spectral balance at 0:50; it is not an aligned first solo attack. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf (PDF pp. 21–22)

transitions.title: Short replies carry the longer span
transitions.how: Solo passagework and short orchestral replies continue to alternate. The bass redirects the harmony while the same flute-and-strings resources remain in play. This map division groups the middle episodes; it does not identify a new theme or claim that every orchestral return begins at the displayed time.
transitions.evidence: The manuscript supports alternating solo and ensemble textures. The report changes at 2:30, but no score alignment identifies the precise written join; the map deliberately groups several exchanges.

transitions.title: The recorded texture withdraws
transitions.how: The surrounding quick movement gives way to a substantially quieter, less densely attacked stretch. The contrast comes from withdrawal rather than a change of metre. The score contains a later suspension before renewed orchestral material, but this timing does not locate an individual fermata or an improvised addition.
transitions.evidence: The report has strong boundaries at 3:58 and 4:02, a level drop of more than 15 dB by 4:05 and reduced attack density through 4:15. The score’s later fermata is visible on manuscript p. 40 (PDF p. 31), without note-level alignment.

transitions.title: Fuller attacks restore the movement
transitions.how: More frequent attacks and a higher recorded level restore the movement’s forward motion. The flute and strings resume the earlier kind of exchange. The contrast with the preceding withdrawal makes the renewed activity clear without requiring a faster tempo.
transitions.evidence: The report’s 4:22 boundary lies between the quiet 4:05–4:15 windows and the renewed 4:25–4:35 activity. The score supplies the returning orchestral material and subsequent solo exchanges; no exact first chord is claimed.

transitions.title: The orchestra gathers the closing gestures
transitions.how: The solo’s extended passagework yields to the shared gestures of the closing tutti. Flute and strings gather the short figures into a G-major cadence, with bass and upper parts coordinating the ending. The change is one of musical role and texture, not the flute falling silent.
transitions.evidence: The critical flute part and first-violin part show the closing tutti together (PDF pp. 29 and 43), clarifying the working manuscript’s shorthand on its final pages. Sustained activity followed by the 6:05 decay supports broad placement only; 5:40 is not an aligned first tutti bar. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf

source.title: C. P. E. Bach, flute-concerto working score, Mus. ms. Bach P 769
source.locator: Presto: PDF pp. 11–39. Read with Kuijken’s introduction and critical performing parts, https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf (PDF pp. 21–22, 29, 40, 43). Blank flute staves are not read as silence: the parts confirm opening and closing tutti participation. These are passage overviews, not note-aligned entries or uninterrupted desk activity. The cello desk represents written basso; actual keyboard or double-bass participation is unestablished.

timeline.note: Opening overview: flute joins strings and written basso in the tutti before its independent solo; the recording includes initial room sound.
Approximate first-solo region: flute elaborates the theme with string and bass accompaniment; individual rests are not mapped.
Middle-passage overview: flute runs alternate with short string interventions. Lit desks need not sound continuously.
Desk activity is deliberately unassigned during the quieter suspension: the audio locates the withdrawal, not the precise solo, fermata or accompanying rests.
Approximate renewed-exchange region: returning string gestures and further flute passagework share the foreground.
Approximate closing region: the critical flute part confirms participation with strings and basso in the final tutti; its first bar is not aligned.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Both sources name the soloist and ensemble. The opened programme does not identify a conductor for this concerto or its continuo player. Credits for soloists in the adjacent Brandenburg concertos have not been transferred to this track. Exact string numbers, keyboard type, double-bass participation and tuning are unestablished.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Flute version of the concerto; complete finale only
fields.note: Only movement III is hosted in this package. Set metadata records part 3 of 3, not possession of the preceding Allegro di molto and Largo. The 1755 date belongs to the original organ concerto Wq 34; the flute adaptation is later and cannot be assigned a precise year. The working manuscript is dated between 1755 and 1768 by Kuijken. The recording’s performing edition, any restored missing bar and the details of a cadenza are unestablished. The modern critical performing parts clarify the manuscript’s shorthand: flute participates in the opening and closing tutti, so a blank flute staff does not establish a rest. These parts are consulted as a reference, not attributed to the 2008 performance or claimed to be public domain. The score-derived orchestra display uses passage overviews rather than aligned entries; the cello desk represents written basso, not a verified allocation of bass instruments.

facts: With his father, Johann Sebastian Bach; law studies at Leipzig and Frankfurt an der Oder
Keyboard player to Frederick II in Berlin and Potsdam, 1740–67 · Hamburg music director, 1768–88
Versuch über die wahre Art das Clavier zu spielen, 1753 and 1762
Wq = Alfred Wotquenne; H = E. Eugene Helm
composer.background:
Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach was the second surviving son of Johann Sebastian Bach and Maria Barbara Bach. He was born in Weimar in 1714; Georg Philipp Telemann was one of his godfathers. The family moved to Cöthen in 1717 and Leipzig in 1723, where his father became Thomaskantor. Emanuel learned the keyboard and composition at home, then studied law at Leipzig and Frankfurt an der Oder. He made music his profession: by 1738 he had entered the circle of the Prussian crown prince Frederick, who became king in 1740.

Frederick played the flute, composed and maintained an orchestra whose leading musicians included Johann Joachim Quantz and the brothers Graun. Bach’s employment was chiefly as a keyboard accompanist. In his own publications he pursued a style independent of the king’s Italianate melodic preferences. His six ‘Prussian’ keyboard sonatas of 1742 and six ‘Württemberg’ sonatas of 1744 put contrasting textures, unexpected rests and highly ornamented slow movements inside the three-movement sonata. The player had to manage changes of character as precisely as changes of fingering.
composer.epithet: A keyboard player who made hesitation, interruption and a change of mind into musical form.
